titulo: The long catch-up: why pay trails prices after an inflation shock

fuente.nota: Escrito para el panel de idiomas. Los datos son aproximados y no deben citarse como fuente.

parrafos: When inflation surged across the rich world after the pandemic, workers discovered an uncomfortable truth about the labour market: pay packets tend to move slowly, while price tags can change overnight. Years later, many households are still trying to recover the purchasing power they lost, and the reasons for that delay say a great deal about how modern economies set wages.

The basic mechanics are not mysterious. Most prices in a market economy are revised continuously, or at least frequently: petrol stations update their boards daily, supermarkets reprice thousands of items every week and energy suppliers pass on wholesale costs within months. Wages, by contrast, are typically fixed for a year or more. Collective agreements in many European countries run for two or three years, and even workers without a union contract usually see their pay reviewed only once a year. When a sudden shock pushes inflation from around 2% to close to 10%, as happened in much of Europe in 2022, the gap between the two clocks opens almost immediately.

Economists call this phenomenon nominal wage rigidity, and it is largely a feature rather than a bug. Long contracts give firms predictability over their costs and spare employees the anxiety of renegotiating every few months. In normal times, when inflation is low and stable, the arrangement costs workers very little. The trouble starts when prices take off unexpectedly. A pay deal signed on the assumption of 2% inflation becomes, in effect, a pay cut once inflation climbs to 8% or 9%, and nobody can reopen the agreement until it expires.

Expectations play a crucial role in the story. Wage negotiators do not simply look backwards at the inflation already recorded; they try to guess what will happen over the life of the next contract. After decades of price stability, both unions and employers were inclined to treat the post-pandemic surge as temporary, a view shared for some time by many central banks. As a result, the first rounds of bargaining delivered increases that, while large by recent standards, fell well short of the rise in the cost of living. Real wages, that is, pay adjusted for inflation, dropped sharply in most advanced economies.

Bargaining power is the second piece of the puzzle. In the 1970s, when a large share of workers belonged to unions and many contracts included automatic indexation clauses, wages chased prices upwards with remarkable speed, sometimes too quickly, feeding the notorious wage-price spiral. Today the picture is very different. Union membership has fallen to well under a quarter of employees in most rich countries, indexation has been dismantled or restricted almost everywhere, and a growing number of people work in sectors where pay is set unilaterally by the employer. Without a mechanism to force a rapid catch-up, workers must rely on the slow grind of annual reviews.

The nature of the shock also matters. The inflation of 2021–23 was driven to a large extent by energy and food, goods that many European economies import. When the price of imported gas soars, the country as a whole becomes poorer: it must hand over more of its output to foreign producers to obtain the same amount of energy. Someone has to absorb that loss. In the short run, it fell mostly on wage earners, since profits in many sectors held up relatively well and, in some cases, even rose. That pattern fuelled a heated debate about so-called ‘greedflation’, the idea that companies had used the turmoil to widen their margins.

The evidence on that point is mixed. Several studies, including work by international institutions, found that profits accounted for an unusually large share of price increases in 2022, particularly in energy, transport and agriculture. Others argue that firms were merely restoring margins squeezed during the pandemic, and that the profit share tends to rise at the start of any inflationary episode before wages respond. What most economists do agree on is the sequence: prices first, profits second, wages last. The question is whether the final stage of the cycle is allowed to run its course.

This is where the dilemma for central banks becomes acute. Once inflation starts to fall, workers naturally seek compensation for the purchasing power they lost. Pay settlements of 4% or 5% may look modest to a household still struggling with its grocery bill, but to a monetary policymaker they can appear dangerously inconsistent with a 2% inflation target, especially if productivity growth remains weak. Raise interest rates too far in response, and the catch-up is cut short; ease too early, and the risk is that higher wage costs feed a second round of price increases. Several central banks have spent much of the past two years walking that tightrope.

Governments have tried a variety of tools to cushion the blow. Some, including Spain, raised the statutory minimum wage substantially, which protected the lowest-paid but did little for those further up the scale. Others opted for energy subsidies, price caps or one-off payments to vulnerable households. Social partners in certain countries struck multi-year agreements that combined moderate increases with review clauses triggered if inflation exceeded a given threshold, a softer and more targeted version of the old indexation schemes. Each approach involves a trade-off between protecting incomes today and avoiding embedding inflation tomorrow.

There is, finally, a distributional dimension that statistics on average wages tend to obscure. Lower-income households spend a larger share of their budgets on food, heating and transport, precisely the items whose prices rose fastest. Their personal inflation rate was therefore higher than the headline figure, while their savings buffers were thinner. Younger workers and those on fixed-term contracts, who often lack the leverage to negotiate, also suffered disproportionately. Conversely, people who changed jobs during the tight labour market of the recovery frequently secured raises well above inflation, suggesting that mobility, rather than loyalty, was the surest path to recovering lost ground.

The broader lesson is that an inflation shock is never neutral. Even when price growth returns to target, the level of prices does not come back down, and the losses incurred along the way are only recovered if wages grow faster than inflation for a sustained period. In much of Europe, real wages have only recently returned to their pre-shock levels, and in some countries they have yet to do so. For policymakers, the episode is a reminder that the credibility of a central bank is built not only on bringing inflation down, but also on convincing citizens that the burden of doing so will be shared fairly.
titulo_es: La larga recuperación: por qué los salarios van por detrás de los precios tras un choque inflacionista
resumen_es: Análisis de por qué los salarios tardan en alcanzar a los precios después de un repunte de la inflación: contratos largos, expectativas, menor poder sindical, naturaleza del choque y dilema de los bancos centrales.

ideas_clave.idea: Since prices are adjusted constantly while pay is usually fixed for a year or longer, a sudden jump in inflation immediately leaves wages behind.
Lengthy pay agreements bring stability and cost little when inflation is low, but an unexpected surge turns agreed rises into real cuts until the deals expire.
Because both sides expected the post-pandemic inflation to be short-lived, early settlements fell well below price growth and real wages declined sharply.
Unlike in the 1970s, weaker unions and the near disappearance of automatic indexation leave workers with no tool for a rapid catch-up.
As the shock came mainly from imported energy and food, it made countries poorer, and the loss fell largely on employees while profits held up, sparking the ‘greedflation’ debate.
Evidence on the role of profits is disputed, but there is broad agreement that prices rise first, profits second and wages last.
Central banks face a dilemma: tightening too much prevents wages from recovering, while easing too soon risks second-round inflation.
Governments used minimum-wage increases, subsidies, price caps, one-off transfers or agreements with review clauses, each involving trade-offs.
Poorer, younger and temporary workers suffered most, whereas those who changed jobs often obtained rises above inflation.
Inflation shocks leave lasting losses because price levels remain higher, and central-bank credibility also depends on sharing the cost of disinflation fairly.

resumen_modelo: The text examines why wages take so long to catch up with prices after an inflationary shock. Its starting point is a difference in timing: whereas most prices are revised constantly, pay is generally set for a year or more through annual reviews or multi-year collective agreements. This rigidity provides stability in calm periods, but when inflation rises unexpectedly, previously agreed increases become real pay cuts that cannot be renegotiated until contracts expire. Moreover, negotiators initially assumed that the post-pandemic surge would be temporary, so the first settlements lagged well behind the cost of living. Workers’ weaker bargaining position compounds the problem: unlike in the 1970s, union density is low and automatic indexation has largely disappeared. The author also stresses the nature of the shock. Since it stemmed mainly from imported energy and food, it made European economies poorer, and the loss fell largely on employees while profits proved resilient, which gave rise to a contested debate on ‘greedflation’. Once inflation eases, central banks face a dilemma between allowing wages to recover and preventing second-round effects, while governments have resorted to minimum-wage rises, subsidies or review clauses, each with drawbacks. The impact has been uneven, hitting low-income, young and temporary workers hardest. In conclusion, the article argues that such shocks are never neutral and that a central bank’s credibility also rests on a fair distribution of the cost of bringing inflation down.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: According to the article, collective agreements in many European countries typically last for a single year.
preguntas.cita: Collective agreements in many European countries run for two or three years
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que los convenios colectivos duran dos o tres años; lo que se revisa una vez al año es el sueldo de quienes no tienen convenio. Se ha cambiado el detalle, así que es falsa.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 2 una expresión que signifique «una característica deliberada, no un defecto».
preguntas.pregunta: Find an expression meaning ‘an intended characteristic rather than a flaw’.
respuestas: a feature rather than a bug
preguntas.cita: it is largely a feature rather than a bug
preguntas.explicacion: La expresión procede de la informática («es una característica, no un error») y se usa para decir que algo aparentemente negativo es en realidad intencionado.

preguntas.pregunta: Why did the first wage settlements after the post-pandemic surge fall short of inflation?
opciones: Because governments imposed legal limits on pay rises
Because negotiators expected the rise in prices to be temporary
Because employers refused to negotiate with unions
Because productivity had collapsed during the pandemic
respuestas: Because negotiators expected the rise in prices to be temporary
preguntas.cita: both unions and employers were inclined to treat the post-pandemic surge as temporary
preguntas.explicacion: El texto atribuye la insuficiencia de las primeras subidas a que ambas partes creían que la inflación sería pasajera. No menciona límites legales ni una negativa a negociar, y la productividad aparece en otro contexto.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: In the 1970s, automatic indexation clauses helped wages keep up with prices quickly.
preguntas.cita: many contracts included automatic indexation clauses, wages chased prices upwards with remarkable speed
preguntas.explicacion: El texto explica que en los años setenta muchas cláusulas de indexación automática hacían que los salarios siguieran a los precios con gran rapidez, a veces demasiada.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 4 una expresión que signifique «el proceso lento y laborioso».
preguntas.pregunta: Find an expression meaning ‘the slow, tedious process’.
preguntas.cita: workers must rely on the slow grind of annual reviews
preguntas.explicacion: «Grind» designa una tarea pesada y monótona; «the slow grind» subraya lo lenta y trabajosa que es la recuperación mediante revisiones anuales.

preguntas.pregunta: Why does a rise in the price of imported gas make a country poorer as a whole?
opciones: Because it reduces the number of hours people work
Because the country must give more of its output to foreign producers for the same energy
Because domestic energy companies go bankrupt
Because the central bank has to raise interest rates
respuestas: Because the country must give more of its output to foreign producers for the same energy
preguntas.cita: it must hand over more of its output to foreign producers to obtain the same amount of energy
preguntas.explicacion: Es un deterioro de la relación real de intercambio: hace falta entregar más producción al exterior para obtener la misma energía. Las demás opciones no aparecen en el texto como causa.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: All the studies mentioned conclude that companies deliberately raised prices to exploit consumers.
preguntas.cita: The evidence on that point is mixed.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que la evidencia es dispar: unos estudios hallan un peso inusual de los beneficios y otros creen que las empresas solo recuperaban márgenes. No hay unanimidad.

preguntas.pregunta: What sequence of events do most economists agree on, and what does it imply for wages?
respuestas: Most economists agree that prices rise first, then profits, and wages only at the end. This implies that workers recover their losses only if this last phase is allowed to continue.
preguntas.cita: What most economists do agree on is the sequence: prices first, profits second, wages last.
preguntas.explicacion: La respuesta debe recoger el orden (precios, beneficios, salarios) y la idea de que la recuperación salarial depende de que se permita completar el ciclo.

preguntas.pregunta: What risk does the article associate with central banks easing policy too early?
opciones: That higher wage costs cause a second round of price rises
That governments lose control of public debt
respuestas: That higher wage costs cause a second round of price rises
preguntas.cita: ease too early, and the risk is that higher wage costs feed a second round of price increases
preguntas.explicacion: Relajar demasiado pronto podría provocar efectos de segunda ronda. Frenar la recuperación salarial es el riesgo contrario (subir demasiado los tipos); el paro y la deuda no se mencionan.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Spain’s minimum-wage increases were financed through a special tax on energy companies.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto menciona que España subió con fuerza el salario mínimo, pero no dice nada sobre cómo se financió ni sobre impuestos a las energéticas.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 9 una palabra que signifique «capacidad de presión o influencia (para negociar)».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning ‘power to influence a negotiation’.
preguntas.cita: who often lack the leverage to negotiate
preguntas.explicacion: «Leverage» significa aquí poder de negociación o influencia; en finanzas también significa «apalancamiento».

preguntas.pregunta: Why does the author claim that an inflation shock is never neutral?
respuestas: Because even when inflation returns to target, prices stay at a higher level, so the losses suffered by workers are only made up if wages outpace inflation for a long time. The burden is also unevenly distributed.
preguntas.cita: the level of prices does not come back down, and the losses incurred along the way are only recovered if wages grow faster than inflation
preguntas.explicacion: La clave es distinguir entre la tasa de inflación y el nivel de precios: aunque la tasa baje, los precios no retroceden y la pérdida de poder adquisitivo persiste.

tribunal.pregunta: Could you briefly explain why wages adjust more slowly than prices?
tribunal.pista_es: Comprensión: resumir la diferencia de calendario entre precios y salarios.
ideas: Prices are revised daily, weekly or monthly
Wages are set annually or in multi-year agreements
Contracts cannot be reopened before they expire

tribunal.pregunta: What is the difference between nominal and real wages, and why does it matter here?
tribunal.pista_es: Definir conceptos y aplicarlos al texto.
ideas: Nominal wages are the amount paid in money
Real wages are adjusted for inflation and measure purchasing power
A nominal rise below inflation is a real cut

tribunal.pregunta: Why are wage-price spirals less likely today than in the 1970s?
tribunal.pista_es: Explicar el cambio institucional en la negociación colectiva.
ideas: Lower union membership
Abolition or restriction of indexation
More credible, independent central banks anchoring expectations

tribunal.pregunta: Do you think the ‘greedflation’ debate is justified?
tribunal.pista_es: Opinión matizada con argumentos de ambos lados.
ideas: Profits rose in some sectors such as energy
Firms may have been rebuilding margins
Market power and competition policy matter

tribunal.pregunta: How did wages and inflation evolve in Spain during this episode, and what role did the minimum wage play?
tribunal.pista_es: Relacionar con España: salario mínimo, convenios y pacto de rentas.
ideas: Large increases in the statutory minimum wage
Multi-year agreement between unions and employers with moderate rises and review clauses
Energy measures such as the Iberian exception

tribunal.pregunta: How should the European Central Bank weigh wage growth when setting interest rates?
tribunal.pista_es: Política monetaria: efectos de segunda ronda frente a recuperación del poder adquisitivo.
ideas: Risk of second-round effects
Importance of productivity growth
Credibility and anchoring of expectations
Distributional consequences of tightening

tribunal.pregunta: Should governments bring back wage indexation to protect workers?
tribunal.pista_es: Opinión sobre política de rentas, con ventajas e inconvenientes.
ideas: Indexation protects purchasing power
It can entrench inflation and spirals
Targeted alternatives: review clauses, transfers to vulnerable households
